name: Mediterranean Landscapes: Preferences and Ecosystem Services
description: Faithful replication of the visual questionnaire in Bidegain, López, González, Martínez-Sastre, Ravera & Cerda (2020), "Social Valuation of Mediterranean Cultural Landscapes: Exploring Landscape Preferences and Ecosystem Services Perceptions through a Visual Approach", Land 9(10):390, using the 16 landscape photographs of Sierra Morena (Andalusia, Spain) from its Figure S2 and the six landscape-unit photographs of its Figure 2. Participants (1) rank the 16 photos, shown in random order, in the paper's three steps: their four favourites, their four least liked, then the middle eight, giving each photo a score from 16 (most preferred) to 1 (least preferred), as in the paper's Table 1; (2) choose their reasons (scenic beauty, subsistence, affinity, cultural/patrimonial value, ecological value, sense of place); (3) score how much each of six landscape types (dehesa, non-tillage olive grove, ploughed olive grove, pine forest, Mediterranean forest, mosaic) supplies 15 ecosystem services from 0 (nothing) to 4 (very much), with the paper's Table S7 definitions; (4) answer the sociocultural questions of Table S4. In the original study (389 local people and 33 experts), four stakeholder groups preferred different landscapes, and dehesas and mosaics were seen as supplying the most ecosystem services. Differences from the original study: (1) online and self-completed instead of face-to-face interviews with printed photos; (2) the paper lists the sociocultural variables (Table S4) but not their exact wording, so those questions are worded by us, and the social-ecological sector is replaced by an optional place-of-residence question; (3) the six landscape units are rated one at a time in random order. Photographs are used with credit for research and removed if the authors object.
author: Bidegain, López, González, Martínez-Sastre, Ravera & Cerda

elements.name: ecosystem_services

items.help: Products derived from the olive grove.
Pastures and feeding areas for livestock which allow to obtain derived products of livestock.
Products derived from uncultivated ecosystems that are consumed by humans for various purposes: medicinal resources, fruits, mushrooms, tubers…
Materials from nature to produce consumer goods: wood, cork, pulp, textile fiber, timber, fuel…
Capacity of ecosystems to reduce the effects of fires, prevent their expansion and encourage regeneration.
Ability of vegetation to trap soil particles carried in the air or water, controlling erosion and desertification and allowing agricultural uses.
Capacity of ecosystems to maintain water quality and its cycle.
Capacity of ecosystems to absorb CO2, regulate the water cycle and control temperatures.
Organisms that transport pollen or seeds; pollinators and dispersers are essential for the maintenance of crops and wild vegetation.
Regulatory capacity of pests and disease vectors of humans, crops and livestock.
Relationships of humans to ecosystems leading to experiential knowledge based on practices, customs and beliefs, transmitted between generations.
Nature is a setting for outdoor activities (bird watching, trekking, sports…) and provides opportunities for tourism (eco-tourism, agro-tourism).
Ecosystems are a scene of hunting and fishing activities.
Ecosystems are a laboratory for experimentation and development of knowledge; they inform us on the functioning of ecological processes and their social function.
